body.objective: Students will be able to explore Greek theatre.
successCriteria: I can describe the features of Greek theatre
I can explain the role of the chorus and masks
I can connect Greek conventions to theatre today
body.hook: Twenty-five centuries ago, up to 15,000 Athenians sat on a hillside to watch plays about gods, kings and terrible choices. They invented the words we still use: theatre, drama, chorus, tragedy and comedy.

vocabulary.definition: A large open-air theatre with curved seating built into a hillside.
A group of performers who speak, sing or move together and comment on the action.
A drama in which the main character suffers a downfall, often through a flaw.
A drama that ends happily and often mocks people or society.
Excessive pride that leads to a tragic hero's downfall.
The release of emotion the audience feels at the end of a tragedy.
An accepted practice in theatre that the audience understands.

study.title: Gods, Masks and the Chorus
study.question: What did Greek theatre look like, and how does it still shape theatre?
study.passage:
Context: Greek theatre grew from festivals for the god Dionysus in Athens in the 5th century BCE. Playwrights competed for prizes. Famous playwrights: Aeschylus, Sophocles ("Oedipus Rex," "Antigone"), Euripides (tragedy) and Aristophanes (comedy).
The theatre: Open-air amphitheatre with excellent acoustics; the orchestra (circular dancing space) for the chorus; the skene (building behind) for entrances and as a backdrop.
Conventions: Only men performed; actors wore large masks showing character and emotion and helping the voice carry; violence happened offstage and was reported; the chorus (12 to 15 people) commented, questioned and spoke for the community.
Activity 1 (10 minutes): Read the summary of "Antigone": she buries her brother against King Creon's law. Identify the tragic hero, the flaw and the catharsis.
Activity 2, Chorus work (25 minutes): In groups of six, create a choral ode responding to Antigone's arrest. Speak in unison, split lines, use echo and canon, and move as one. Wear neutral half-masks or make simple paper masks.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; history summarized from standard theatre history sources.
steps: Read the context of Greek theatre
Learn the theatre space and conventions
Create and perform a choral ode
discussion: Why might masks have been necessary in a huge open-air theatre?
What does the chorus give the audience that the characters can't?
Is Creon or Antigone the tragic hero?
Where do you see chorus-like devices today (musicals, film narrators)?
study.product: Perform a one-minute choral ode for a modern issue in the style of a Greek chorus, then write a paragraph connecting two Greek conventions to modern theatre or film.

examples.title: Hubris
examples.answer: He refuses to change his law even when warned, leading to tragedy

examples.title: Chorus role
examples.problem: What does the chorus do in "Antigone"?
examples.answer: Comments on the action and voices the community's views
examples.explore: How is this like a narrator?

examples.title: Masks
examples.problem: Why did Greek actors wear masks?
examples.answer: To show character clearly to a huge audience and let few actors play many roles
examples.explore: What do masks take away from acting?

examples.title: Offstage violence
examples.problem: Why was violence reported, not shown?
examples.answer: It was a theatre convention; messengers described it, letting the audience imagine

practice.q: What was the orchestra in a Greek theatre?
practice.a: The circular space where the chorus performed.
It happened offstage and was reported by a messenger.
King Creon's law against burying her brother.
Unison, split lines, echo, canon or unified movement.

practice.q: Why were masks useful in a large amphitheatre?
practice.a: They showed character clearly and helped voices carry; few actors could play many roles.

practice.q: Who is the tragic hero of "Antigone"? Justify.
practice.a: Either can be argued; Creon's hubris causes the downfall of his family.

practice.q: Name a modern device similar to the Greek chorus.
practice.a: Narrators, ensembles in musicals or voice-overs.

practice.q: How does Greek tragedy still influence stories today?
practice.a: Flawed heroes, moral dilemmas and downfall plots appear in film and TV.

misconceptions: Thinking Greek theatre was performed indoors like today
Thinking the chorus just sang background songs
Thinking tragedy means any sad story
